title: Entity & Tax Structure Setup: LLC, S-Corp or Holding Company

slides.title: Title, operator, and tax treatment are three separate choices, and your lender often makes the first
slides.subtitle: Lesson PA.10. Entity & Tax Structure Setup: LLC, S-Corp or Holding Company
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice.
slides.notes:
Somebody has already told you to put your rental in an LLC. Somebody else probably said to run it through an S-corp. This lesson sorts those answers out.

By the end you'll be able to separate three questions people blur together. Who holds title? Who operates the rental? How is the activity taxed? You'll know which professional answers each one, and where each name shows up in the paperwork.

You'll leave with a filled decision worksheet and a list of questions for your attorney, CPA, insurer, and lender.

I won't give you a universal recommendation, because there isn't one. The right structure depends on your state, your lender, your insurer, your partners, and your tax facts. Cedar Ridge is hypothetical, and nothing here is legal, tax, lending, or insurance advice.

slides.title: Title owner, operator, and tax treatment are three questions with three answers
rows: Whose name is on the deed. That person or entity signs as the buyer.
Who holds the Airbnb account, the permit, the cleaner and co-host agreements, and the payouts
How the IRS classifies the entity and activity, which forms get filed, how income and losses reach you

box.label: The rule for layers
box.text: All three can be you and your spouse, personally. Or all three can differ. Every layer you add has a cost and a paper trail. Add one only when it solves a problem you can name.

slides.notes:
Here are the three questions.

First, title owner. Whose name is on the deed? That person or entity owns the property and signs as the buyer.

Second, operator. Who runs the rental business? That's whoever holds the Airbnb account, signs the cleaner and co-host agreements, holds the permit, and collects the payouts.

Third, tax treatment. How does the IRS classify the entity and the activity? That decides which forms get filed and how income and losses flow to you.

'Put it in an LLC' answers the first question. 'Run it through an S-corp' answers the third. Neither one answers the question your lender asks first, which is who's borrowing.

These can all be the same, you and your spouse. Or a property LLC might hold title while an operating company runs the listing. Every layer costs money and paperwork. Add one only when it solves a problem you can name.

slides.title: An LLC is a legal form under state law, and an S-corp is a federal tax election

left.head: Limited liability company
items: You file with the state and pay its fees
State law decides the liability protection
The SBA says ownership, liability, taxes, and filing rules vary by state

right.head: S corporation
items: An LLC can be taxed as a C corp or an S corp
The LLC files Form 2553 to elect it
Form 2553 also counts as electing corporate classification (Pub 3402)
Shareholder-employees must get reasonable pay before distributions

slides.notes:
This is the distinction that clears up most of the confusion.

A limited liability company is created under state law. You file with the state and pay the state's fees. The state's law decides what liability protection you get. The SBA says an LLC separates business and personal liabilities, and that the rules vary by state.

An S corporation is a tax status. The SBA says designations like S corp aren't strictly business structures. An LLC can be taxed as a C corp or an S corp.

To become an S corp, the LLC files Form 2553. IRS Publication 3402 says that filing also counts as electing corporate classification, so you don't file Form 8832 first.

People usually want an S-corp to manage self-employment or payroll taxes on active business income. The IRS requires reasonable pay to a shareholder-employee before non-wage distributions. That means payroll and a second return. For a single STR, that's a CPA question.

slides.title: An LLC's default federal tax treatment depends on how many members it has
rows: Disregarded. Activity shows on the owner's return, such as Schedule C or E.
LLC filing as a corporation or partnership
The IRS respects treating it as disregarded or as a partnership.
S corporation. Corporate classification is deemed elected.
slides.caption: Community property states named by the IRS: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. Outside them, a spouse-owned two-member LLC is generally a partnership.

box.label: Before you put real estate in an S corporation
box.text: Ask the CPA to explain what happens later when you move the property out, refinance, or sell.

slides.notes:
The IRS lays out the defaults in Publication 3402.

A one-member LLC is disregarded unless it elects otherwise. Its activity shows on the owner's own return, such as Schedule C or Schedule E.

A domestic LLC with two or more members is a partnership by default. It files Form 1065.

Married couples have one extra wrinkle. In community property states, the IRS will respect spouses treating a jointly owned entity as either disregarded or a partnership. Those states are on the slide. Outside them, a two-member LLC owned by spouses is generally a partnership. Your CPA decides which applies to you.

And one warning. If anyone suggests putting the real estate itself inside an S corporation, ask the CPA to walk you through moving the property out, refinancing, and selling. Get that answer before you choose it.

slides.title: Your loan type often settles who holds title before you pick an entity
rows: Borrowers must be natural persons, with limited exceptions such as certain land trusts
Expect title and the note in your personal names
Each lender sets its own rules. Kiavi says some DSCR lenders allow an LLC.
Ask whether a personal guarantee is required, in writing

box.label: If a guarantee is required
box.text: The LLC doesn't separate you from the loan debt. It may still separate you from some other claims. Your attorney explains what it does and doesn't do in your state.

slides.notes:
Your financing choice from PA.7 often settles the title question before you pick an entity.

Conventional loans sold to Fannie Mae generally go to individuals. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide requires borrowers to be natural persons, with limited exceptions like certain land trusts. If Maya and Chris take the conventional quote, expect title and the note in their personal names.

DSCR lenders set their own rules. Kiavi says some DSCR lenders allow borrowing through an LLC. That's one lender's page, not a market standard.

An entity loan may also require a personal guarantee from the owners. I couldn't confirm a lender's published guarantee terms, so put that question to your lender in writing.

If a guarantee is required, the LLC doesn't separate you from the loan debt. It may still help with some other claims. Your attorney tells you what it does in your state.

slides.title: Decide the entity before closing, because retitling later can trip the due-on-sale clause

nodes.d: With your attorney, CPA, lender, and insurer.
Lender, title company, and insurer, in writing.
Every document shows the names you chose.
A transfer to your LLC isn't on the federal exceptions list.

box.label: If you must move title later
box.text: Get the lender's written consent before you deed the property anywhere. Ask your title company whether the transfer affects your owner's title policy.

slides.notes:
Now the caution about moving title after closing.

A mortgage or deed of trust usually has a due-on-sale clause. It lets the lender demand full payment if the property is transferred without consent.

Federal law, 12 U.S.C. 1701j-3, lists transfers a lender can't treat as a trigger on certain residential loans. Examples include some transfers to a spouse or into certain living trusts. A transfer to your own LLC is not on that list. Some lenders will consent to it, and some won't.

So get the lender's written consent before you deed the property anywhere. And ask your title company whether the transfer affects your owner's title policy.

The better path is on the slide. Decide before closing, so the lender, title company, and insurer all draw up documents with the same names. Retitling after closing costs money and can put the loan and the title coverage at risk.

slides.title: Insurance follows the named insured, so ask the insurer four direct questions
items: Who should be the named insured if title sits in an LLC?
Can both the LLC and the individual owners be named?
Does the policy cover the operating company, if it's a separate entity?
Does the lender need to be listed as mortgagee, and in what exact name?

box.label: Umbrella, LLC, or both
box.text: An umbrella liability policy is another way to handle liability. Which fits you is a joint call for your attorney and insurer. AirCover for Hosts doesn't replace your own policy.

slides.notes:
Your STR policy protects the named insured. Say title sits in an LLC and the policy names you personally. You may have a gap when you file a claim. The reverse is a problem too.

So ask the insurer these four questions, directly and in writing.

Who should be the named insured if title sits in an LLC? Can both the LLC and the owners be named? Does the policy cover the operating company, if that's a separate entity? Does the lender need to be listed as mortgagee, and in what exact name?

Airbnb tells hosts they're responsible for their own insurance and should review coverage and exclusions. It also says AirCover for Hosts doesn't replace it.

An umbrella liability policy is another way people handle liability. Whether an umbrella, an LLC, or both fits your situation is a joint call for your attorney and your insurer.

slides.title: Map every closing document to one name, because mismatches break claims later
rows: The title owner, or an assignment clause if you're forming the LLC
Individual owners, if the lender requires it
slides.notes:
Draw this map before closing. Every document should match the structure you chose. Mismatches are how a claim, a permit renewal, or a tax filing goes sideways.

This first half covers the purchase itself.

The purchase contract names the buyer. If you're still forming the LLC, your attorney may use an assignment clause. The deed names the title owner. The promissory note names whoever the lender approved as borrower. The mortgage or deed of trust is signed by the title owner, pledging the property.

If the lender requires a personal guaranty, the individual owners sign it. The title policies name the title owner and the lender. The STR insurance policy names the insured and the mortgagee.

Walk down this column with your PA.10 worksheet open. If two rows disagree, fix it before closing, not after.

slides.title: The operator's name goes on the platform, permit, and vendor accounts
rows: The entity that earns the income

box.label: Beneficial ownership
box.text: FinCEN's March 2025 interim final rule exempts US-created entities from BOI reporting. Check the page before you form.

slides.notes:
The second half of the map is the operation.

The permit and tax registration go in whatever name the local office requires. Often that's the owner or the operator. The Airbnb and Vrbo accounts, the payout method, and the platform tax forms go to the operator. The bank account belongs to the entity that earns the income. Vendor agreements are signed by the operator.

A note on beneficial owners. The federal reporting rule used to apply to most small LLCs. FinCEN's March 2025 interim final rule exempts entities created in the United States and their owners. That status has changed before, so check FinCEN's page before you form an entity. Your bank will still ask who owns and controls the LLC.

FinCEN also reports that a court vacated its residential real estate reporting rule in March 2026. Your title company tracks what applies to your closing.

slides.title: Ten personal days sits under both personal-use thresholds at 212 rented nights
slides.side:
Under IRS Publication 527, a dwelling counts as a home when personal use exceeds 14 days or 10% of fair-rental days, whichever is greater.

With any personal use, Pub 527 still requires dividing expenses between rental and personal use.
slides.notes:
Sam's PA.5 walks through cost segregation and year-one depreciation. That lesson assumes the CPA has already settled some facts. Here's what drives them. The entity choice doesn't change most of this.

Start with personal use. Maya and Chris plan about 10 personal days a year. Under IRS Publication 527, a dwelling is used as a home when personal use exceeds 14 days or 10% of fair-rental days, whichever is greater.

At 212 rented nights, 10% is 21.2 days. So 10 personal days sits under both thresholds, on these assumptions.

But Publication 527 still requires dividing expenses between rental and personal use whenever there's any personal use. Here that's roughly 212 of 222 total days, or 95.5% rental.

Bring back from Sam's PA.5 the depreciation figures. Your CPA uses this day count alongside them.

slides.title: A 3.5-night average stay changes which tests the CPA applies, and no entity does the hours

left.head: Average stay (IRS Pub 925)
items: 7 days or less: not a rental activity under the passive rules
The 'STR loophole' is really a set of tests with facts
Your hours and your cleaner's or co-host's hours matter
The CPA applies the tests

right.head: Same days, different offices
items: A beach house the owner occupies over 14 days next year isn't treated as non-owner-occupied
That's a lending-disclosure rule, not a tax rule
Tell your lender and your CPA the same honest number

slides.notes:
Next, average stay. Under IRS Publication 925, an activity isn't a rental activity for the passive rules if the average customer stay is 7 days or less. Cedar Ridge averages 3.5 nights.

That changes which participation tests the CPA applies. It's the reason people talk about 'the STR loophole.' It's really a set of tests with facts behind them.

Whether your losses can offset W-2 income depends on participation facts. The hours you work matter. So do the hours your cleaner or co-host works. The CPA applies the tests. Your entity doesn't do those hours for you.

One more note for the lender. The CFPB's Regulation Z commentary says a beach house the owner will occupy over 14 days next year isn't treated as non-owner-occupied under that rule. That's a lending rule, not a tax rule. Same personal-use days, different offices. Give both the same honest number.

slides.title: Send your CPA eight written questions before you choose an entity
items: Which participation tests apply, given our average stay and hours? How should we log time?
Does our personal-use plan require dividing expenses, and on what day count?
Schedule E or Schedule C, given the services we provide guests?
If title goes into a one- or two-member LLC, which return is filed, and what does it cost?
Is an S-corp election useful at all? If it holds real estate, what happens at refinance or sale?
How do cost segregation and bonus depreciation from PA.5 interact with our entity and hold period?
Does the entity limit a future sale or 1031 exchange? (OP.12 covers exits.)
What records do you want from day one: bank account, bookkeeping software, mileage, time log?
slides.notes:
Take these questions to your CPA in writing. Written questions get written answers, and you'll want those answers later.

The first two are about facts: which participation tests apply and how to log your time, and whether your personal use means dividing expenses.

The third is about which schedule the activity reports on. That depends on the services you provide guests.

The fourth and fifth are about entities. Which return gets filed if title goes into an LLC, and what it costs to prepare. And whether an S-corp election helps at all.

The sixth connects to Sam's PA.5. Cost segregation and bonus depreciation interact with your entity and how long you'll hold.

The seventh looks at the exit. OP.12 covers that. The eighth is what records the CPA wants from day one. Set those up before your first booking.

slides.title: For a first property, a holding company often adds cost before it solves anything
slides.text: For a first property, a holding company often adds cost before it solves anything.
slides.support: Revisit it in OP.11 when you buy property number two. Ask your attorney whether your state offers a series LLC, and how your lender and insurer treat it.
slides.notes:
You'll hear about holding companies next. A holding company structure usually means a parent LLC that owns several property LLCs. People use it to keep each property's liabilities separate while managing them together.

For a first property, it often adds cost before it solves anything. You'd be paying for filings and returns on entities that don't have a second property to protect yet.

So park it. Revisit it in OP.11 when you're buying property number two.

When you get there, ask your attorney whether your state offers a series LLC. Then ask your lender and your insurer how they treat one. Those two answers often matter more than the structure chart.

slides.title: Cedar Ridge has three workable structures, and each one waits on professional answers
rows: DSCR only, if the lender lends to LLCs; guarantee likely
Operating LLC under a written agreement
Partnership (1065) unless a community property exception applies
Depends on the operating LLC's members and elections
LLC plus insurance; limits depend on state law and guarantee
Operator liability separated, property still personal
Lender's entity terms; guarantee; named insured
Whether it holds up and what it costs
slides.notes:
Maya and Chris are married, both on W-2 income, with their primary home in personal names. In the base case they self-manage with a local cleaner.

Here are three options, laid out for their professionals. None of these is my recommendation. Each one depends on answers they don't have yet.

Option A keeps everything in their personal names. It fits either loan. Liability is handled with insurance plus an umbrella.

Option B puts title in Cedar Ridge LLC on a DSCR loan. That works only if the lender lends to LLCs, and a guarantee is likely. By default it's a partnership return, unless a community property exception applies.

Option C keeps title personal and puts the operation in a separate LLC under a written agreement. The open question is whether that arrangement holds up and what it costs to maintain.

Next, let's price Option B.

slides.eyebrow: Cedar Ridge · the cost of Option B
slides.title: Option B's LLC costs about $1,625 a year, which leaves $127 on the PA.9 numbers
slides.side:
Canonical base case: $5,572 - $1,625 = $3,947, about $329 a month instead of about $464.

PA.9 revised base case: $1,752 - $1,625 = $127 a year.

side_box.label: The real question
side_box.text: Is the liability benefit worth about $1,625 a year to this household? Their attorney and insurer can tell them.

slides.notes:
Let's put a number on Option B. Assume a $300 state annual report fee, a $125 registered agent, and $1,200 for a partnership return. All three are assumptions. That's $1,625 a year. State filing fees vary widely, so replace the $300 with your state's actual fee.

Against the canonical DSCR base-case cash flow of $5,572, Option B drops it to $3,947. That's about $329 a month instead of about $464.

But remember PA.9. After diligence, the base case was already down to $1,752. Option B's $1,625 would take it to $127 a year.

That doesn't make Option B wrong. It means the liability benefit has to be worth about $1,625 a year to this household. Their attorney and insurer are the people who can tell them whether it is.

slides.title: Ask every professional from one worksheet so they all work from the same facts
slides.text: Fill in Part 1 first: your states, owners, financing path, personal-use days, average stay, hours, and umbrella policy.
rows: Do you lend to an LLC? Which types? Is a personal guarantee required?
Will you consent to a transfer to an LLC after closing, in writing?
What exact names go on the note, mortgage, and mortgagee clause?
What protection does an LLC give in this state, given a guarantee?
Formation and annual fees; registered agent; operating agreement terms
Does a later transfer affect title insurance or trigger transfer tax?
Who should be the named insured? Can we add the LLC and ourselves?
Whose name must the permit and tax registration be in?
slides.notes:
Here's the exercise. It has three parts, and you fill it out before your first call with any professional.

Part 1 is facts. Which state the property sits in and which state you live in. Who owns what percentage. Whether you're married, and whether it's a community property state. Your financing path from PA.7. Personal-use days, average stay, who does the operating work and roughly how many hours. Other properties you own or plan. Any umbrella policy.

Part 2 is this slide: questions by professional. Three for the lender, three for the attorney, two for the insurer, the CPA's eight, and one for the licensing office.

Bring the whole worksheet to all four meetings. The point is that the lender, the attorney, the insurer, and the CPA are all working from the same facts. Write each answer down with a date.

slides.title: Record each structure decision with one reason, one confirmer, and a date
rows: Bank account and bookkeeping setup date

box.label: The closing rule
box.text: The lender, title company, and insurer need the same names in writing a week before closing. If they don't have them, don't close until they do.

slides.notes:
Part 3 is the decision itself. Five rows.

Title owner at closing. Operator. Tax classification. How you'll cover liability, whether that's an entity, insurance, an umbrella, or some mix. And the date you'll set up the bank account and bookkeeping.

For each one, write the choice, one sentence on why, who confirmed it, and the date.

Then apply the rule at the bottom. The lender, the title company, and the insurer need the same names in writing a week before closing. If they don't have them, don't close until they do.

That rule sounds strict. It's much cheaper than fixing a mismatched deed, loan, and insurance policy after the fact.

slides.title: Five professionals each own one piece of the structure decision
rows: **Real estate attorney in the property's state**
Liability protection an entity gives, how to form it, the operating agreement, whether any transfer is advisable
Tax classification, any S-corp election, which return reports the activity, participation and personal use, exit consequences
Which borrowers it lends to, any guarantee, exact names on loan documents, its position on later transfers
Named insured, additional insureds, mortgagee clause, umbrella coverage
Whose name must be on the STR permit and lodging tax registration
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what.

Your real estate attorney, licensed in the property's state, confirms what liability protection an entity gives, how to form it, what the operating agreement says, and whether any transfer makes sense.

Your CPA confirms the tax classification, whether an S-corp election makes sense, which return reports the activity, participation and personal-use treatment, and what happens at exit.

Your lender confirms, in writing, who it lends to, whether a guarantee is required, the exact names on the loan documents, and its position on transfers after closing.

Your insurer confirms the named insured, any additional insureds, the mortgagee clause, and umbrella coverage.

The licensing office and the state tax agency confirm whose name goes on the permit and the lodging tax registration.

slides.title: Get the names settled in writing this week, before closing documents are drawn
items: Fill in Part 1 of the worksheet with your facts.
Email your lender the three lender questions and ask for written answers.
Email your insurer the four named-insured questions.
Send your CPA the eight questions and book a call.
slides.next: Next: PA.11 Closing Day: Documents, Wire Fraud Prevention & Possession. Bring your completed worksheet to check every name on every document.
slides.notes:
Four things this week. Each one takes under an hour.

First, fill in Part 1 of the worksheet. Just the facts.

Second, email your lender the three lender questions. Ask for written answers.

Third, email your insurer the four named-insured questions.

Fourth, send your CPA the eight questions and book a call. Give them a few days with the list before you talk.

With the names settled, you're ready to close. PA.11 Closing Day walks through the closing figures line by line against your loan quote. It covers how to move the money safely and what to collect when you get the keys. Bring your completed worksheet. You'll use it to check every name on every document at the table.

These are the main sources behind this lesson. The full list is in the PA.10 sources section. It adds the IRS S corporation compensation page, the Kiavi DSCR guide, the CFPB's Regulation Z commentary, FinCEN's real estate rule page, and Airbnb's hosting pages.

The tax classification rules come from IRS publications and pages. The legal-form point comes from the SBA. The borrower rule for conventional loans comes from Fannie Mae's Selling Guide. The due-on-sale exceptions come from the federal statute.

Each one was checked on September 25, 2026, through a search summary of the official page. Open them yourself before you rely on them. FinCEN's reporting rules in particular have changed more than once.

The Cedar Ridge entity costs are assumptions. Replace them with your state's real fees.
